newsitem.title: USA: Clinton dines with governors Sunday, meet Monday.
newsitem.headline: Clinton dines with governors Sunday, meet Monday.

text.p: President Clinton hosted state governors at a White House dinner Sunday night ahead of a Monday morning meeting, pledging to deepen and enrich his partnership with his former colleagues.
Clinton, who was governor of Arkansas until he was elected president in 1992, has long-standing ties to many governors as well as an interest in the policy issues that dominate their working days.

In a pre-dinner toast, Clinton pledged "to continue the partnership we have had, to try and deepen it and to enrich it, and beginning tomorrow, to try to listen to you and your concerns and hear your advice."
On Monday, he was to hold a roundtable with them at 9:15 a.m. EST which the White House said was likely to cover issues ranging from welfare reform to the Medicare and Medicaid health care programs.
On many of these matters, Clinton and the governors do not agree.

The governors, who began a four-day Washington meeting of the National Governors Association Saturday, said they would oppose any Clinton plan to cap funding for the Medicaid health care program for 37 million poor, elderly and disabled.
"All of us are joined at the hip and opposed to the caps," Ohio Republican Gov. George Voinovich said Saturday.
On Sunday, White House chief of staff Erskine Bowles told reporters the White House was committed to imposing spending limits on Medicaid despite opposition from governors.

Clinton and Republican governors also disagree on his plan to revisit last year's welfare reform law that ended the 61-year federal guarantee of aid to the poor and gave the states broad power to design their own welfare programs.

On Saturday, Republican governors voted to oppose a draft governor's association policy statement asking Congress to restore benefits to some legal immigrants who will lose Food Stamps and federal disability aid under the law.

Clinton administration officials, supported by some state governors with large immigrant populations, have said they plan to ask Congress to restore more than $16 billion in spending cuts under the law to restore such benefits.
Bowles Sunday shrugged off the opposition by the Republican governors to reopening the law. "We're not going to be able to agree on all things at all times," he said.
